title: Patterns: a first taste of regular expressions
summary: Search for a shape instead of a word: any digit, the start of a line, four digits in a row.

scheme: c.t      cat, cut, c9t: . is any character
lo*g     lg, log, loog: * repeats o
text: A regular expression (regex) describes the shape of a text, not one exact word. grep, sed and awk all understand them.
- A few characters have a special meaning: ^ start of the line, $ end, . any character, * the one before, 0 or more times.

scheme: lo+g      log, loog, but not lg
text: Square brackets give a list of allowed characters: [0-9] is any one digit.
- A ^ just inside the brackets means "not": [^ ] is one character that isn't a space.
- grep -E (extended) adds handy repeats: + means one or more, {4} exactly four, | means or.
- Always put the pattern in single quotes, so the shell passes * and the brackets to grep untouched.
Build a pattern piece by piece, reading the text you want: four digits, a dash, two digits, a dash, two digits.
- ^ in front keeps only the lines that start with a date.
- Test it on the file with grep before you use it anywhere else.

scheme: grep -E '[0-9]+' f       lines with a number
text: The same patterns work in sed and awk, which you'll meet next.
- sed -E uses them to find what to replace.
- awk puts one between slashes to pick the lines to work on. It needs no -E: it always understands + {4} |.
That's enough regex for daily work: start simple, and add a piece only when you need it.
